newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria seen on course for EMU - committee report.
newsitem.headline: Austria seen on course for EMU - committee report.

text.p: Austria has succeeded in reining in its public debt and should have few problems complying with the Maastricht rules for European economic and monetary union (EMU), the state finance committee said on Monday.

In a report, the committee forecast public debt would decline to 67 percent of gross domestic product this year from 70 percent in 1996. That leaves Austria short of Maastricht's 60 percent reference level "but fulfils the spirit of the treaty", it said.
The committee also predicted a small regional budget surplus this year would help reduce a central government deficit of 68 billion schillings, or 2.7 percent of GDP.
"Austria has achieved significant success in cutting its budget deficit and has reached a turning point," committee chairman Helmut Frisch told a news conference.
"This year the deficit will come in at less than (the required) three percent."
The report put 1996 public debt at a provisional 1,692 billion schillings, or 70 percent of GDP, up from 1,630 billion schillings, or 69.3 percent, the previous year.
Central government's 1996 budget deficit fell to 93.7 billion schillings, or 3.9 percent of GDP, from 123.5 billion schillings, or 5.3 percent, the previous year.

To reduce public debt this year the government can draw on some 17 billion schillings raised by the privatisation of the Creditanstalt bank and 75 billion schillings from the hiving off of road construction agency ASFINAG.
It will save around 10 billion schillings by removing water fund Wasserwirtschafts-fond from the budget.

Foreign currency debt accounted for 20.9 percent of the total 1,417 billion schillings financial debt last year. The committee said a shift towards marks and guilders was a deliberate strategy ahead of the introduction of the euro.

Repayments in 1996 stood at 107.6 billion schillings, of which 86.5 billion were interest payments. That compared with total payments of 118.6 billion schillings the previous year, of which 81.5 billion were interest payments.
For this year the committee forecast interest payments of 91.9 billion schillings -- exceeding the planned budget deficit for the first time since 1992.
"That is proof that the budget cuts are paying off," Frisch said. -- Vienna newsroom, +43-1 531 12 254
